title: NFTs & Decentralized Applications
tagline: Build, store, sell and sell honestly: ERC-721 collections, metadata, marketplaces, front ends and responsible practice
summary: A practical, honest guide to NFTs: what a token really contains, collection contracts with supply, price, limits and royalties, allowlists and soulbound credentials, IPFS and on-chain storage, a marketplace contract, a front end with ethers, mint economics and the legal, safety and ethical questions around them. All Solidity and JavaScript listings were checked. This course gives education, not legal or investment advice.

modules.title: NFT fundamentals
modules.summary: What an NFT really is, what ownership means, what lives on and off the chain and why metadata matters.
modules.outcome: You can explain precisely what an NFT contains, what ownership does and does not mean and where the data lives.
modules.intro: NFTs have been hyped and mocked in equal measure. Strip away both and you find a simple tool: a unique entry in a public ledger. This module explains exactly what that entry is, what it is not, and why the answer matters when you build or buy.

topics.title: A unique entry in a ledger
topics.html:
An NFT (non-fungible token) is an entry in a smart contract's ledger that says: token number 7 in this contract is owned by this address. Because the ledger is public and the rules are in the contract, anyone can check who owns token 7, see its full history of owners and know that no copy of that exact entry exists.

Fungible versus non-fungible
Fungible (ERC-20)Non-fungible (ERC-721)
ExampleA 100-rupee noteA numbered concert ticket
Interchangeable?Yes: any note will doNo: seat 12A is not seat 40B
Ledger entryaddress → amounttoken id → owner
Typical questionHow much do I have?Which ones do I have?
Definition

Smart contract ownership. Ownership of an NFT means your address is recorded as the owner in the contract. It lets you transfer or use the token. It does not by itself give you the copyright to any picture, any legal title or any promise from the creator.

Check what you just learned

1. What does owning an NFT mean?
  • Your address is recorded as the owner of that token in the contract (correct)
  • You own the copyright of the artwork
  • You own the website
  • You own the blockchain

A ledger entry, not a legal right by itself.

Tip

Whenever you read about an NFT, ask: what exactly does the owner get? The answer is in the contract and in the written terms, not in the picture.

Check what you just learned

1. ERC-721 maps:
  • address to amount
  • token id to owner (correct)
  • name to price
  • gas to ETH

Every id has one owner.
keyPoints: An NFT is a unique token id owned by an address in a contract.
Owning the token is not owning the copyright.

topics.title: What is on-chain and what is not
topics.html:
Where the pieces live
PieceUsually storedWhy
Token id and ownerOn the chainThat is the ledger itself
Contract rules (supply, royalty)On the chainCode and constants
tokenURI (a link)On the chainA short string
Metadata JSON (name, description, attributes)Off-chain, found through the linkCheaper
Image, audio or videoOff-chain, found through the metadataLarge files cost too much on-chain
Licence termsIn legal text, linked from the projectLaw is outside the chain

This chain of pointers is where NFTs break. If the link, the metadata file or the image disappears, the token still exists but shows nothing. The strength of an NFT therefore depends on how well each pointer and file is protected, which the storage module covers in detail.

Check what you just learned

1. What happens if the image link stops working?
  • The token is deleted
  • The owner changes
  • The token still exists but may show nothing (correct)
  • The contract is destroyed

The pointer breaks, not the ledger.

Check what you just learned

1. tokenURI returns:
  • The price
  • The image bytes
  • The owner's key
  • A link to metadata (correct)

It returns a pointer, not the file.
keyPoints: Ownership lives on-chain; large files usually live elsewhere.
A broken link leaves a token that shows nothing.

topics.title: Metadata and the marketplace view
topics.html:
Fields in the JSON
FieldPurpose
name and descriptionShown by wallets and marketplaces
imageA link to the artwork; ipfs:// links point to content-addressed storage
external_urlA page with more details
attributesTraits used for filters and rarity, each with a trait type and value

Marketplaces and wallets look for these standard field names. If you follow the convention, your tokens will display properly almost everywhere. If you invent your own names, tools will not know what to show.

Check what you just learned

1. Why follow the standard metadata field names?
  • Wallets and marketplaces know how to display them (correct)
  • It is required by law
  • It saves gas
  • It hides the image

Compatibility.

Check what you just learned

1. The attributes list is used for:
  • Fees
  • Traits and filters (correct)
  • Mining
  • Passwords

Rarity and search.

Key terms: flip and sort

NFT
A non-fungible token
Token id
The unique number of a token in a contract
Metadata
Descriptive data about a token
tokenURI
A link to a token's metadata
Fungible
Interchangeable
Attribute
A trait of a token
keyPoints: Metadata JSON has name, description, image and attributes.
Standard names make tokens display correctly in every app.

modules.title: Building NFT contracts
modules.summary: A complete collection contract with supply, price, limits, royalties and withdrawal, plus allowlists and soulbound tokens.
modules.outcome: You can build and explain a capped collection contract, an allowlist mint and a non-transferable credential.
modules.intro: A good NFT contract is short and strict: it enforces the promises made to buyers. This module builds one from the ground up with OpenZeppelin and then shows two common variations.

topics.title: A collection contract, line by line
topics.html:
What each protection does
LineProtects against
MAX_SUPPLY and totalMintedCreating more tokens than promised
msg.value != mintPrice * quantityUnderpayment and accidental overpayment
mintedBy and MAX_PER_WALLETOne buyer taking everything
_safeMintTokens lost in contracts that cannot handle them
onlyOwner on withdrawStrangers taking proceeds
_setDefaultRoyaltyDeclares the creator's royalty for marketplaces that honour it
supportsInterface overrideLets wallets discover that the contract supports both ERC-721 and ERC-2981

Common mistakes

  • Setting the price in the front end only and not checking it in the contract.
  • Forgetting a supply cap and promising scarcity anyway.
  • Letting the owner change the metadata after minting without telling buyers.

Check what you just learned

1. Why check the payment in the contract?
  • It is required by the wallet
  • It is cheaper
  • Front ends can be bypassed by calling the contract directly (correct)
  • It hides prices

The contract is the only enforcer.

Check what you just learned

1. MAX_PER_WALLET reduces the risk that:
  • The owner changes
  • Gas rises
  • Events vanish
  • One buyer takes the whole collection (correct)

It spreads the collection more fairly.
keyPoints: A collection contract enforces supply, price and limits itself.
Never rely on the web page to enforce rules.

topics.title: Royalties and their honest limits
topics.html:
ERC-2981 lets a contract declare how much the creator should receive on a resale: for example 500 out of 10,000, which is 5%. It is only a declaration. The standard does not move any money. The marketplace must read the value and pay it. Many marketplaces do; some make royalties optional; and a buyer who trades privately pays none.

Ways to handle royalties
ApproachStrengthWeakness
Declare with ERC-2981Standard and simpleOptional for marketplaces
Use your own marketplace with enforced royaltiesFull controlYou must build and secure it, and attract users
Restrict transfers to approved marketplacesCan enforce royaltiesLimits where holders can sell and has been controversial
Do not rely on royaltiesHonest and simpleIncome must come from the first sale or other services

Royalty calculator

Change the sale price and the royalty rate to see the creator's income. A teaching tool.

Adjust Sale price (rupees), Royalty (%), Marketplace fee (%) and see Creator royalty (rupees), Marketplace fee (rupees), Seller receives (rupees) change.

Check what you just learned

1. Does ERC-2981 guarantee that royalties are paid?
  • No: it only declares the rate and marketplaces choose whether to pay it (correct)
  • Yes always
  • Yes on all chains
  • Only for art

A declaration, not enforcement.

Check what you just learned

1. A 500 out of 10,000 royalty is:
  • 50%
  • 5% (correct)
  • 0.5%
  • 500%

Basis points.
keyPoints: ERC-2981 declares a royalty; it does not enforce it.
Plan income without depending on royalties.

topics.title: Allowlists and soulbound tokens
topics.html:
The allowlist stores only a Merkle root. Each supporter receives a proof for their address from the project's website. This is the same technique as a Merkle airdrop, applied to minting rights.

Soulbound tokens
FeatureWhy
Cannot be transferredA credential should stay with the person it was issued to
Issuer can revokeMistakes and fraud need a correction path
Overrides _updateAll transfers pass through it in OpenZeppelin 5
PrivacyNever put personal data in a public token; use a number or hash

Check what you just learned

1. Why should a certificate be non-transferable?
  • To save gas
  • It hides the owner
  • It should stay linked to the person who earned it (correct)
  • It is required by ERC-721

Credentials are personal.

Watch out

A soulbound token on a public chain makes a person's credentials publicly visible. Consider privacy, consent and what happens if a wallet is lost.

Check what you just learned

1. An allowlist root stored on-chain is:
  • A fee
  • A list of every address
  • A private key
  • 32 bytes representing the whole list (correct)

A single root stands for the whole list.

Key terms: flip and sort

Mint
Create a token
Supply cap
The maximum number of tokens
ERC-2981
The royalty declaration standard
Allowlist
A list of addresses allowed to mint
Soulbound
Non-transferable
Basis points
Hundredths of a percent
keyPoints: Merkle allowlists give early supporters guaranteed mints.
Soulbound tokens block transfers and need privacy care.

modules.title: Metadata and storage
modules.summary: Content addressing and IPFS, on-chain art, reveals and the honest durability of each approach.
modules.outcome: You can choose a storage strategy, build on-chain metadata and explain its costs and risks.
modules.intro: The most common way an NFT fails is not a hack; it is a missing file. This module shows how to choose storage that lasts and how to build NFTs that carry their own art.

topics.title: Content addressing and IPFS
topics.html:
A normal web address says where a file is: the server and path. If the server changes the file or disappears, the link breaks or shows something else. A content address says what the file is: it is a cryptographic hash of the content itself. Change one byte and the address changes. IPFS, the InterPlanetary File System, uses content addresses, so a link of the form ipfs:// followed by a hash always refers to exactly the same bytes.

Location versus content
Web addressContent address (IPFS)
Names...A placeThe exact content
Can the content change silently?YesNo: the address would change
Who must keep it available?The server ownerAnyone who stores (pins) it
Failure modeBroken link or swapped fileFile not found if nobody keeps a copy

Content addressing guarantees that a file has not been changed, but it does not guarantee that the file is still available. Someone must pin it, which means promising to keep a copy. Serious projects use several independent pinning services, keep their own copies and may use networks designed for long-term storage.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a content address guarantee?
  • The file has not been changed (correct)
  • The file is always available
  • The file is private
  • The file is free

Integrity, not availability.

Check what you just learned

1. Pinning means:
  • Deleting a file
  • Keeping a copy available (correct)
  • Encrypting a file
  • Selling a file

Someone must store it.
keyPoints: Content addresses identify exactly what a file contains.
Integrity is guaranteed; availability needs pinning.

topics.title: Fully on-chain NFTs
topics.html:
Trade-offs of fully on-chain storage
BenefitCost
Survives as long as the chain doesStorage is expensive: roughly 22,100 gas per new 32-byte word
No dependence on any serverLimited to small images, usually simple vector art
Art can respond to on-chain dataMore code means more risk
Strongest durability claimHarder to build and test

Check what you just learned

1. Why is on-chain art usually small vector graphics?
  • It looks better
  • Wallets cannot show photos
  • Storing large files on-chain is very expensive (correct)
  • It is a rule

Every byte costs gas.

Check what you just learned

1. Base64 is used to:
  • Sign data
  • Encrypt data
  • Compress data
  • Encode data into text for data: links (correct)

Text-safe encoding.
keyPoints: On-chain NFTs build their own metadata and art in tokenURI.
They are very durable but limited by cost.

topics.title: Reveals, freezing and trust
topics.html:
Many collections mint first and reveal the artwork later, to stop buyers sorting by rarity before the mint ends. This creates a trust problem: until the reveal, the metadata is a placeholder, and the owner decides when and what to reveal. Buyers have to trust the creator not to swap better tokens for themselves.

Ways to make a reveal fairer
TechniqueHow it helps
Commit to a provenance hash in advancePublish a hash of all final metadata before minting so it can be checked later
Randomised offsetShift token ids by a random number chosen after minting ends
Freeze the metadataOnce revealed, the contract permanently disables further changes and announces it
Publish the full set openlyAnyone can compare against the committed hash

What to tell buyers

  1. Whether metadata can change, and who can change it.
  2. When and how the reveal happens.
  3. Where files are stored and who pins them.
  4. Whether and when the metadata will be frozen.
  5. What happens if a pinning service closes.

Check what you just learned

1. What does a provenance hash let buyers check?
  • That the revealed set matches what was committed before minting (correct)
  • The price
  • Who minted first
  • The gas fee

No quiet swapping.

Check what you just learned

1. Freezing metadata means:
  • It is deleted
  • It can no longer be changed (correct)
  • It is hidden
  • It is cheaper

The change becomes permanent.

Key terms: flip and sort

Content address
A name derived from the content itself
IPFS
A content-addressed file network
Pinning
Keeping a copy of a file available
Base64
A way to write bytes as text
Reveal
Publishing final metadata after minting
Provenance hash
A hash of the full collection committed in advance
keyPoints: Reveals need trust; provenance hashes and freezing reduce it.
Tell buyers exactly who can change what.

modules.title: Marketplaces and dApps
modules.summary: A fixed-price marketplace contract, approvals, a front end with ethers, and reading events.
modules.outcome: You can follow and build a simple marketplace flow, write a minting front end and use events to list tokens.
modules.intro: An NFT contract alone is not a product. People need a page where they can connect a wallet, mint, view and trade. This module builds a small marketplace contract and the front-end code that talks to it.

topics.title: A fixed-price marketplace
topics.html:
Design decisions
DecisionReason
The NFT stays with the seller until soldNo escrow contract holds the token; simpler and safer for sellers
Pull payments for proceedsA seller who cannot receive ETH cannot block a sale
Effects before interactionsThe listing is deleted before the transfer, preventing reuse
nonReentrantA second layer against reentrancy
Exact price requiredAvoids stuck funds
Watch out

This contract is a teaching example. It does not check that the seller still owns the token at sale time beyond the transfer failing, and it has no royalties, fees or auctions. A real marketplace needs much more design and an audit.

Check what you just learned

1. Why delete the listing before transferring the NFT?
  • To save gas
  • To hide the price
  • So the listing cannot be reused during a callback (correct)
  • It is optional

Checks-effects-interactions.

Check what you just learned

1. The marketplace needs the seller to:
  • Burn the token
  • Give it the private key
  • Pay a deposit
  • Approve it on the NFT contract (correct)

Otherwise it cannot move the token.
keyPoints: A marketplace lists, sells and credits proceeds with approvals.
Delete listings first and use pull payments.

topics.title: A front end with ethers
topics.html:
What the code does
StepWhy
BrowserProvider(window.ethereum)Connects to the wallet the user already has
getSignerAsks the wallet for permission to act as the user
Read mintPrice from the contractNever hard-code prices that can differ from the contract
Contract call with valueSends the transaction; the wallet shows details and asks to confirm
tx.wait()Waits until the transaction is mined
queryFilter with Transfer eventsFinds which tokens an address received

Good dApp habits

  • Show the contract address and the network.
  • Handle rejection and errors with friendly messages.
  • Disable the button while waiting.
  • Never ask for more approvals than needed.
  • Never ask for a recovery phrase.
  • Link to the verified contract on a block explorer.

Check what you just learned

1. Why read the price from the contract?
  • The page might show a different price from what the contract requires (correct)
  • It is faster
  • Wallets demand it
  • It saves gas

The contract is the source of truth.

Check what you just learned

1. tx.wait() waits for:
  • The wallet to open
  • The transaction to be mined (correct)
  • The price to change
  • A refund

Confirmation.
keyPoints: Connect, read, send, wait and show results.
The contract is the source of truth; the page is a helper.

topics.title: Events and indexing
topics.html:
A contract cannot easily list 'all tokens owned by this address' without loops that cost too much. Instead, apps read events. Every mint or transfer emits a Transfer event with the sender, recipient and token id. A front end can ask the node for those events, or use an indexer: a service that reads events from the chain and stores them in a database so pages can query quickly.

Options for reading data
OptionGood forLimit
Contract view functionsSingle values: owner of token 7Not good for lists
queryFilter on eventsSmall projects and recent historySlow over long ranges
A hosted indexer or subgraphMarketplaces, profile pages and filtersAnother service to run or trust
Your own database fed by eventsFull controlYou maintain it

Common mistakes

  • Looping over all token ids in a view function and hitting limits.
  • Trusting an indexer without checking the chain for important decisions.
  • Forgetting that very recent blocks can be reorganised.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use events to list a user's tokens?
  • Wallets ban loops
  • Contracts cannot store anything
  • Events are free to read and record transfers (correct)
  • Events are encrypted

They are the cheap way to build lists.

Check what you just learned

1. An indexer is:
  • A fee
  • A wallet
  • A token
  • A service that reads events into a database (correct)

Fast queries.

Key terms: flip and sort

Marketplace
A contract or site for trading NFTs
Approval
Permission for a contract to move a token
Listing
An offer to sell at a price
dApp
A decentralised application
Event
A log entry emitted by a contract
Indexer
A service that organises events for queries
keyPoints: Events record transfers; apps use them or indexers to build lists.
For important decisions, verify against the chain.

modules.title: Utility, business models and honest design
modules.summary: Where NFTs genuinely help, how mints make or lose money, and how to design for lasting value.
modules.outcome: You can judge whether an NFT fits a use case and build a simple mint budget.
modules.intro: The best NFT projects solve a real problem; the worst are speculation with a picture attached. This module helps you tell them apart and plan the money honestly.

topics.title: Where NFTs genuinely help
topics.html:
Use cases and honest assessments
Use caseWhy a token helpsCaution
Certificates and credentialsAnyone can verify without calling the issuerPrivacy and revocation; may be soulbound
Event ticketsUnique, verifiable, resale rules possibleLost wallets and fraud support
Memberships and accessHolding the token unlocks accessAccess must be enforced by the app
Digital art and collectiblesProvenance and a marketCopyright and speculation
Game itemsPortable items across gamesDepends on games choosing to support them
Supply-chain recordsShared, tamper-evident historyGarbage in, garbage out at the point of entry

In each case the value comes from something outside the token: an institution that stands behind it, a community that values it or an application that honours it. The token is the verifiable receipt; it is not the value by itself.

Check what you just learned

1. Where does an NFT's lasting value come from?
  • What people, institutions or apps do with it (correct)
  • The token itself alone
  • Its gas cost
  • Its id number

Value comes from real use.

Check what you just learned

1. A credential NFT is useful because:
  • It is expensive
  • Anyone can verify it (correct)
  • It is secret
  • It is random

Public verifiability.
keyPoints: NFTs help when public verification or portability matters.
Value comes from what stands behind the token.

topics.title: Mint economics
topics.html:
Mint budget

Change the supply, price and sell-through to see revenue and profit. A teaching model with made-up numbers.

Adjust Supply, Price (rupees), Sold (%), Costs (rupees) and see Revenue (rupees), Profit (rupees), Break-even NFTs change.

Costs that are easy to forget

  • Development and testing.
  • Security review.
  • Art, writing and design.
  • Legal advice and company set-up.
  • Storage and pinning for years, not days.
  • Support, community management and moderation.
  • Network fees for deployment and updates.

Common mistakes

  • Planning for a sold-out mint and ignoring the case where half sells.
  • Promising future features you cannot fund.
  • Spending the whole raise before delivering the first product.

Check what you just learned

1. Why plan for a partial sell-through?
  • Sellouts are impossible
  • Gas depends on it
  • Real mints often sell less than hoped, and costs still have to be paid (correct)
  • It is required

Budget for the realistic case.

Check what you just learned

1. Break-even is:
  • Royalty
  • Price minus cost
  • Supply
  • Costs divided by price, rounded up (correct)

Number of sales needed.
keyPoints: Budget revenue, costs and break-even; plan for partial sales.
Do not forget storage, support and legal costs.

topics.title: Designing for lasting value
topics.html:
Principles

  1. Start with a real need, not with the token.
  2. Make the promise small and keep it.
  3. Store files in ways that outlive the project.
  4. Be open about who can change what.
  5. Give holders something useful over time, not just at the mint.
  6. Plan how the project can end gracefully.
Warning signs of an unsustainable project
SignWhy
Value depends on new buyers arrivingIt fails when they stop
Anonymous team with large insider holdings and no vestingNo accountability
Roadmaps of grand promises with no budgetUnderdelivery
Pressure to buy nowManipulation
Fake volumeWash trading hides lack of demand
Watch out

Nothing in this course is investment advice. NFTs can lose all their value, and most do. Never spend money you cannot afford to lose.

Check what you just learned

1. Why plan how a project can end?
  • Holders deserve a clear outcome, such as frozen metadata and archived files (correct)
  • Projects never end
  • Gas requires it
  • Marketplaces demand it

A graceful end protects holders.

Check what you just learned

1. Wash trading is:
  • Cleaning wallets
  • Trading with yourself to fake demand (correct)
  • A royalty
  • A mint

It deceives buyers about real demand.

Key terms: flip and sort

Utility
What a token lets you do
Provenance
A verifiable history
Sell-through
The share of supply that sells
Break-even
The point where income covers costs
Wash trading
Trading with oneself to fake demand
Roadmap
A plan of future work
keyPoints: Start with a need; keep small promises; store files durably.
Plan for the project's end as well as its launch.

modules.title: Safety, law and ethics
modules.summary: Scams, security habits, copyright and licences, privacy and environmental and ethical questions.
modules.outcome: You can write an honest buyer notice, recognise common scams and explain rights and licences clearly.
modules.intro: NFTs attract creators, collectors and criminals. A professional project protects its community from scams, tells the truth about what buyers get, respects artists and thinks about its wider effects.

topics.title: Scams and safe habits
topics.html:
Common NFT scams
ScamHow it worksDefence
Approval phishingA fake mint site asks you to approve a contract that then drains your NFTsCheck the site and the contract; use a separate wallet for minting; review approvals
Fake collectionsA copy with the same name and images but a different contractUse the official link and verify the contract address
Free airdrop trapsAn unexpected NFT carries a link that leads to a malicious siteIgnore and never interact with unknown tokens
ImpersonationFake support or admins ask for your recovery phraseNobody legitimate will ask for it
Wash trading and fake volumeTrades between related wallets create false hypeLook at real, independent holders
Rug pullsCreators sell out or abandon the project after the mintCheck the team, the contract powers and the delivery record

Personal safety habits

  • Use a hardware wallet for anything valuable.
  • Keep a separate wallet for experiments and minting.
  • Read every wallet prompt before you sign.
  • Revoke old approvals regularly.
  • Never share your recovery phrase.
  • If something feels rushed, stop.

Check what you just learned

1. Why use a separate wallet for minting?
  • It is cheaper
  • It hides your address
  • A drained experimental wallet does not take your valuable assets with it (correct)
  • Wallets require it

Limit the damage.

Check what you just learned

1. A legitimate project will never ask for:
  • Your email
  • Your public address
  • Your feedback
  • Your recovery phrase (correct)

Never share it.
keyPoints: Approval phishing, fake collections and impersonation are common.
Separate wallets, careful reading and revoking approvals protect you.

topics.title: Copyright, licences and honest sales
topics.html:
Buying an NFT of an artwork does not by default transfer the copyright of that artwork. Unless the seller says otherwise in writing, the buyer owns the token, and the creator keeps the copyright. Good projects publish a clear licence stating what holders may do: display the work, make personal copies, perhaps use it commercially within limits.

Licence ideas
Licence ideaWhat holders can do
Personal display onlyShow the work in wallets and galleries
Personal and limited commercialUse the work in small merchandise or content up to a revenue limit
Full commercial rightsUse the work freely, which the creator must clearly grant
Public domain dedicationAnyone can use the work, including non-holders
Honest sales checklist
ItemWhy
State what the buyer gets and does not getAvoids misleading buyers
Do not promise profits or price risesSuch promises are unreliable and often unlawful
Disclose who holds large amountsConcentration is a risk
Explain who can change the contract or metadataTrust must be informed
Respect other people's workDo not sell NFTs of art you do not have the right to sell
Take legal advice for your countryRules differ and change

Check what you just learned

1. Does buying an NFT of an artwork transfer its copyright by default?
  • No: copyright stays with the creator unless the terms say otherwise (correct)
  • Yes always
  • Only on weekends
  • Only for photos

Read the licence.

Watch out

This lesson is educational, not legal advice. Laws about copyright, consumer protection and digital assets differ by country.

Check what you just learned

1. A written licence should state:
  • The gas price
  • What holders may do with the work (correct)
  • The block number
  • The wallet brand

Clear rights.
keyPoints: Token ownership is not copyright; a licence defines holder rights.
Sell honestly: say what buyers get and do not get.

QuestionConsiderations
PrivacyPublic chains are permanent; never put personal data in a token or its metadata, and think about linking wallets to identities
ConsentIssuing credentials to people publicly needs their agreement
EnvironmentMost major chains now use far less energy than earlier proof-of-work designs; still, check the chain you use and say so honestly
AccessibilityWallets and fees exclude many people; offer alternatives where it matters
ArtistsDo not copy or sell other people's work; pay creators fairly
Exit and supportHave a plan for lost wallets, mistakes and project end

Responsible builders ask not only 'can we do this?' but 'should we, and who might be hurt?' A credential system that makes sensitive information public, or a collection that misleads buyers, can cause real harm even if the code is perfect.

Check what you just learned

1. Why avoid personal data in token metadata?
  • It costs gas
  • Wallets cannot show it
  • Public chains are permanent and anyone can read it (correct)
  • It is slow

You cannot take it back.

Tip

A good habit: write down the worst thing that could happen to a user of your project and what you will do to prevent and handle it.

Check what you just learned

1. On a public chain, data you write is:
  • Encrypted by default
  • Private
  • Deletable
  • Practically permanent (correct)

Think before you write.
